questions.q: A quiz asks four office-holders: a member of a municipal corporation, a Rajya Sabha member, a Vidhan Sabha member and the Vice President. How many of the four reached office through indirect elections?
questions.a: Two: the Rajya Sabha member and the Vice President
o: Two: the Rajya Sabha member and the Vice President
Three: all except the Vidhan Sabha member
One: only the Vice President
Four: all of them, as every post is filled by some vote

questions.q: The Eco Club of a school has had only one candidate for president for three years, and the teacher says, 'Nobody objected, so the members are exercising their choice.' Which idea from the chapter does this overlook?
questions.a: Choice needs at least two contestants, so a lone candidate gives no real choice
o: Choice needs at least two contestants, so a lone candidate gives no real choice
Choice is exercised only when the president is elected indirectly
Choice matters for the Rajya Sabha but not for a school club
Choice is complete once a vote is held, whoever stands

questions.q: A resident says, 'My vote is just one among lakhs, so it cannot make my MLA answerable to me.' Which reply best fits the chapter's account of the vote?
questions.a: The vote is the principal means of electing and holding representatives accountable
o: The vote is the principal means of electing and holding representatives accountable
The vote only decides who sits in the Rajya Sabha, so it cannot reach an MLA
Accountability comes from the Speaker, not from voters at all
A single vote matters only when the election is indirect

questions.q: Kiran reads that the Gram Panchayat in her village was elected in 2022 and the Lok Sabha in 2024. Using the five-year rule for directly elected bodies, which pair of next election years is correct?
questions.a: Panchayat 2027 and Lok Sabha 2029
o: Panchayat 2027 and Lok Sabha 2029
Panchayat 2029 and Lok Sabha 2027
Panchayat 2027 and Lok Sabha 2027
Panchayat 2026 and Lok Sabha 2028

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A government cannot continue beyond its prescribed term without seeking the people's mandate again.
Reason (R): Elected representatives are accountable to the people, and periodic elections are how that accountability is ensured.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about how representatives reach office.
1. Members of local bodies such as Panchayats and municipal corporations are elected through direct elections every five years.
2. The Vice President is chosen when citizens vote directly for that office.
3. In an indirect election, citizens vote for representatives who then choose or elect the leaders.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Which of these situations would the chapter treat as a failure of the principle behind periodic elections?
questions.a: A Vidhan Sabha stays in power well past its term with no fresh vote
o: A Vidhan Sabha stays in power well past its term with no fresh vote
A new Lok Sabha is chosen after its five years end
A Panchayat holds its election on schedule
A Rajya Sabha member is chosen by elected representatives

questions.q: A Vidhan Sabha was directly elected in 2023. Counting a five-year term, voters face the next election in the year ___.
True or False: A government that has completed its prescribed term can carry on without seeking the people's mandate again, provided it is performing well. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the answer to whether a government can continue beyond its term without the mandate is No, because periodic election of those who decide on our behalf is crucial and representatives stay accountable to the people.
s: Reason: the right to elect and hold representatives accountable is ensured only through periodic elections, whatever the performance

questions.q: Differentiate between a direct and an indirect election, and give one office from India for each.
questions.a: In a direct election citizens vote straight for their representative, for example a Lok Sabha member. In an indirect election citizens vote for representatives who then choose the leader, for example the Vice President.
s: Direct: citizens vote for the representative or leader themselves; one correct office
Indirect: citizens vote for representatives who choose the leader; one correct office

questions.q: Gurmat was elected class representative in Grade 8. (a) Should she continue as CR in Grade 9 without a fresh election? (b) Which feature of a government does this match, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) No, because classmates must be able to choose again. (b) A government cannot continue beyond its prescribed term without seeking the people's mandate again.
s: (a) No, with the reason that the electors must choose again
(b) Matches a government needing a fresh mandate after its term

questions.q: Bina says, 'In my town three posts are filled by election: the Lok Sabha member, the ward councillor and the Rajya Sabha member.' (a) Which two of these are chosen by direct election? (b) Why is the third different?
questions.a: (a) The Lok Sabha member and the ward councillor of the local body. (b) The Rajya Sabha member is elected indirectly, since citizens do not vote for that office themselves.
s: (a) Lok Sabha member and local body member named as direct
(b) Rajya Sabha is indirect: others choose, not citizens voting for the office

questions.q: A student asks why 'psephology' is the word for the study of elections. Explain the origin of the word and what the study covers.
questions.a: It comes from the Greek psephos, meaning pebble, plus logy, meaning systematic study. Pebbles were used for voting in ancient Greece, and psephology is the scientific study of elections.
s: Greek psephos means pebble and pebbles were used for voting
Psephology is the scientific or systematic study of elections

questions.q: Rohan says, 'We vote only once in five years, so an MP need not answer to us in between.' How far is he right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Voting does happen only at intervals, so it is periodic. But the chapter says elected representatives are accountable to the people and that the periodic vote is how the right to hold them accountable is ensured, so they cannot ignore the voters.
s: The right part: the vote comes at periodic intervals of five years
The wrong part: representatives remain accountable and the periodic vote is the means of holding them to it

questions.q: Write a school-level example for each: one post filled by a direct election and one filled by an indirect election. Say who votes in each.
questions.a: Direct: Head Boy chosen when every student votes. Indirect: Head Boy chosen by class representatives, who were themselves elected by students. In the first the students vote for the person, in the second they vote for those who choose.
s: A direct example where the electors vote for the post-holder
An indirect example where elected representatives choose
Who votes stated correctly for both

questions.q: Explain why 'one party contesting' leaves voters without a real choice, using the chapter's question about a single contesting party.
questions.a: The chapter asks whether we can exercise our choice if only one political party contests and answers No. With one party, voters cannot compare, prefer or reject, so the vote cannot be the means of choosing or holding anyone accountable.
s: States the chapter's answer: No, choice cannot be exercised
Reason: no alternative to compare or prefer
Link to accountability: the vote cannot change or hold anyone to account

questions.q: Justify the statement, 'Regular and periodic elections lie at the core of democracy.' Use the chapter's example of the class representative, the government's term and the idea that the vote is the principal means of choice.
questions.a: Gurmat cannot hold the CR post without a fresh election because classmates must be able to choose again. In the same way a government cannot go beyond its term without a mandate. Representatives decide on our behalf, so they are accountable to us. The right to elect and hold them accountable is ensured through periodic elections, with the vote as its principal means. Without regular elections that right would not be exercised.
s: Applies the government's prescribed term and mandate
Representatives decide on our behalf and are accountable
The vote as the principal means of electing and holding to account
A reasoned conclusion about the core of democracy

questions.q: Compare direct and indirect elections using three offices from the chapter. For each office, state who votes, then explain one reason a country might use direct election for some offices and indirect for others.
questions.a: Lok Sabha: citizens vote directly. Vidhan Sabha and local bodies such as Panchayats: citizens vote directly every five years. President, Vice President and Rajya Sabha: elected indirectly, where citizens vote for representatives who then elect the leaders. A reasoned point: offices that make decisions closest to citizens carry their direct vote, while others are filled by elected representatives who choose, so every office still traces back to the people.
s: Three offices correctly placed as direct or indirect
A reasoned explanation of mixing the two methods

questions.q:
The council of Nandgaon town was elected in March 2021 for the usual five-year term. A flood in 2025 destroyed two bridges, and the council has a Rs 12 crore rebuilding plan underway. In January 2026 the council passes a resolution to postpone the next election by 18 months so that the work is not disturbed. About 48,000 voters live in the town, and a citizens' group objects.
(a) In which month and year was the election due? In which month and year would the council now go to the voters?
(b) Which principle of the chapter does the resolution put at risk, and why?
(c) The council argues continuity helps the flood victims, the citizens argue they must be able to choose again. Decide which should prevail, giving one cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) March 2026; September 2027. (b) The government cannot continue beyond its prescribed term without seeking the people's mandate again: accountability to the people is ensured through periodic elections, so 18 months without it removes the voters' power. (c) Either side with a cost: holding the election on time keeps accountability but may disturb relief work for some weeks; postponing keeps the work steady but leaves 48,000 voters unable to choose or remove the council for 18 months. A defensible judgement is that the election goes ahead on time, because the plan can be continued by whichever council the voters pick.
s: (b) Prescribed term and mandate, with accountability lost
(c) A side taken with a stated cost on the other

questions.q:
A school with 600 students and 20 classes must choose its Head Girl. Option X: every student votes directly, and each vote takes about 2 minutes at a single table. Option Y: the 20 class representatives, each elected earlier by their own class, vote to choose the Head Girl, with a vote taking about 2 minutes each.
(a) Which option is a direct election and which is indirect?
(b) Work out the total voting time in minutes under each option.
(c) How many votes does a candidate need to have more than half of all votes under each option?
(d) Which option would you recommend, and what does your choice give up?
questions.a: (a) X is direct; Y is indirect. (b) X: 600 x 2 = 1200 minutes (20 hours). Y: 20 x 2 = 40 minutes. (c) Over half of 600 is 301; over half of 20 is 11. (d) Either choice with its cost: X gives every student a voice but takes 20 hours of table time; Y is quick but only 20 students choose, so a candidate can win with 11 votes and students depend on their representatives.
s: (d) A recommendation with the cost named

questions.q: In a Lok Sabha constituency three candidates polled 30,000, 28,000 and 22,000 votes. Under the system India uses for the Lok Sabha, what is the result?
questions.a: The 30,000 candidate wins, with 37.5 per cent of the votes polled
o: The 30,000 candidate wins, with 37.5 per cent of the votes polled
No one wins, because nobody crossed 50 per cent
The top two candidates face a second round of voting
All three win seats in proportion to their votes

questions.q: Meena, a graduate in Maharashtra, votes for the Vidhan Parishad. Which method converts her vote into seats?
questions.a: Proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote
o: Proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote
First-Past-The-Post, where the highest vote-getter wins
A two-round contest, with a second round if nobody has over half
Nomination by the Governor, with no counting of votes

questions.q: In the country of Dhanapur the five constituencies each have 1,00,000 valid votes. Party P wins four seats and Party Q one, though Q polled 1,95,000 votes in all and P only 1,65,000. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: Under FPTP the party with the most votes overall need not win the most seats
o: Under FPTP the party with the most votes overall need not win the most seats
Under FPTP the party with the most votes overall always wins the most seats
Under FPTP seats are shared out in proportion to votes
The result shows a mistake in counting the constituencies

questions.q: A student names states that have a Vidhan Parishad. Which of these states is NOT among the six the chapter lists as bicameral?
questions.a: Rajasthan
o: Rajasthan
Karnataka
Telangana
Bihar

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha are elected by the First-Past-The-Post system.
Reason (R): The Rajya Sabha, the President and the Vice President are elected using proportional representation.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about electoral systems and State legislatures.
1. Under FPTP, a candidate must secure more than 50 per cent of the votes polled to win.
2. In six States the legislature has two houses, the Upper House being the Vidhan Parishad.
3. Under proportional representation voters vote for a party, and seats are allotted in proportion to the votes it receives.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Match each electoral method with how it works.
1. First-Past-The-Post
2. Majority system with a second round
3. Proportional representation
4. Single transferable vote
a. Voters vote for a party, and seats follow total votes
b. The candidate with the most votes wins even with under half
c. The top two meet again if no one has more than half
d. Votes of the lowest candidate pass on by second preference
Using the quota formula in the chapter, if 72,000 valid votes are cast to fill 5 seats, the minimum votes needed to win a seat is ___.
Which statement about the single transferable vote counting is NOT part of the chapter's four steps?
questions.a: The candidate with the most votes after the first count is eliminated
o: The candidate with the most votes after the first count is eliminated
Voters mark their preferences on the ballot
The candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated
Votes of the eliminated candidate go to second preferences

questions.q: True or False: Under FPTP the winning candidate must always have more than half of the votes polled. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the candidate with the most votes wins even if those votes are less than 50 per cent of the total polled. The more-than-half rule belongs to the majority system with a second round.
s: Reason: the most votes decide, even under half; more than half is the rule of the second-round majority system

questions.q: A body fills 2 seats and 45,000 valid votes are cast. (a) Using the chapter's formula, find the quota. (b) A candidate is eliminated with the fewest votes; what happens to those ballots?
questions.a: (a) 45,000 / (2 + 1) + 1 = 15,001 votes. (b) Each ballot is transferred to the candidate named as second preference on it.
s: (b) Votes pass on by second preference

questions.q: In Dhanapur, Party R polled 1,40,000 of the 5,00,000 votes (28 per cent) but won no seat under FPTP. (a) What seats would it get in a 100-seat house under proportional representation? (b) Name one reason this is a point in favour of proportional representation.
questions.a: (a) 28 of the 100 seats. (b) Seats follow the share of votes, so a party with a large vote share is not left out.
s: (b) Seats are in proportion to votes so power is shared proportionately

questions.q: Differentiate between the way a voter votes under FPTP and under proportional representation.
questions.a: Under FPTP each voter votes for one candidate in the constituency and the one with most votes wins. Under proportional representation voters vote for a party, not a person, and seats in Parliament are allotted in proportion to the total votes of each party.
s: FPTP: vote for one candidate, most votes wins
PR: vote for a party, seats in proportion to total votes

questions.q: Name two groups that elect members to the Vidhan Parishad, and say who nominates some members and for which fields.
questions.a: Members are elected by the members of the Vidhan Sabha and local bodies, and by graduates and teachers. The Governor nominates some members for fields such as art, science, social service, literature and co-operatives.
s: Two groups of electors correctly named
The Governor nominates, with fields named

questions.q: Ravi claims, 'Both houses of Parliament, the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, are elected by the same FPTP method.' Is he right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The Lok Sabha is elected by FPTP. The Rajya Sabha, along with the President and Vice President, is elected using proportional representation. The mistake is to treat all Parliament as one method.

questions.q: Show that, in an FPTP contest with exactly three candidates sharing all the votes, the winner cannot have only 30 per cent of the votes.
questions.a: If the winner had 30 per cent, the other two would share 70 per cent. Then at least one of them would have 35 per cent or more, more than the winner, which contradicts that the winner has the most votes. So the winner must have more than one-third.
s: Sets the winner at 30 per cent so the rest hold 70
Shows one rival must have at least 35

questions.q: Write three results for one constituency with 1,00,000 votes in which an FPTP candidate wins with less than half the votes, and state the winner's share.
questions.a: Example: A 38,000, B 33,000, C 29,000. A wins with 38 per cent, less than half, because the most votes win.
s: The right winner under the most-votes rule
The winner's share under 50 per cent

questions.q: Country Ratnadweep uses a second round. Round 1 gives X 42 per cent, Y 38 per cent and Z 20 per cent of 2,50,000 votes. In round 2, 70 per cent of Z's voters go to Y and the rest to X. (a) Why is a second round needed? (b) Who wins and with what share? (c) Would FPTP have given the same winner?
questions.a: (a) Nobody got more than 50 per cent in round 1, so the top two, X and Y, compete again. (b) Z's 50,000 voters: 35,000 to Y and 15,000 to X. Y = 95,000 + 35,000 = 1,30,000, which is 52 per cent; X = 1,05,000 + 15,000 = 1,20,000, 48 per cent. Y wins. (c) No: FPTP would have given the win to X with the most votes in round 1.
s: (a) No one had more than 50 per cent, so top two compete again

questions.q: Dhanapur's election gave Q 39 per cent, P 33 per cent and R 28 per cent of votes, but P won 4 of 5 seats, Q 1 and R 0 under FPTP. Using these figures, argue for or against FPTP, and name one thing the opposite view would say.
questions.a: Seat shares are P 80 per cent, Q 20 per cent, R 0 against vote shares 33, 39 and 28. A case against: the party with the most votes got fewer seats than P and 28 per cent of voters have no member. A case for: each constituency has one clearly identified winner, and the system is simple. The opposite view would say proportional representation shares power in proportion to votes. Either side earns marks if it uses the figures.
s: Seat shares and vote shares compared with figures
A position taken with a reason using the data

questions.q:
Two neighbouring regions elect an assembly. Region X has 2,50,000 voters and holds a second round whenever no candidate crosses 50 per cent; the second round costs Rs 4 crore. In round 1 the candidates polled 42 per cent, 38 per cent and 20 per cent.
(a) Who goes into the second round, and how many votes did each of them poll in round 1?
(b) What is the cost of the second round for each voter in Rs?
(c) If a rule of 'most votes wins' were used, who would have won and by how many votes?
(d) A citizens' forum says the second round is worth the cost. Take a side using the figures.
questions.a: (a) The 42 per cent and 38 per cent candidates, with 1,05,000 and 95,000 votes. (b) Rs 4,00,00,000 / 2,50,000 = Rs 160 per voter. (c) The 42 per cent candidate wins by 10,000 votes. (d) For: the winner then holds over half the votes, which no one had in round 1; against: Rs 160 per voter when the leader was ahead by 10,000. Either side with figures is accepted.
s: (d) A side taken using the figures

questions.q:
An electoral body must fill 3 seats through the single transferable vote. 80,000 valid votes are cast, and the first preference count gives A 31,000, B 22,000, C 12,000, D 9,000 and E 6,000.
(a) Find the minimum number of votes needed to win a seat, using the chapter's formula.
(b) Who is declared elected after the first count?
(c) E is eliminated and 4,000 of E's votes go to C and 2,000 to D. Then D is eliminated, and 8,000 of D's votes go to C. Does C reach the winning number?
(d) A member says plain FPTP would have been simpler for this contest. Judge this with one point for and one against.
questions.a: (a) 80,000 / (3 + 1) + 1 = 20,001. (b) A (31,000) and B (22,000) cross it. (c) C: 12,000 + 4,000 = 16,000, then D has 9,000 + 2,000 = 11,000 and is eliminated; C gets 8,000 more = 24,000, which is above 20,001, so C is elected. (d) For FPTP: counting is simple, the top three would be A, B and C. Against: the transfers let voters' second preferences count and no vote is wasted on a candidate who is eliminated. Either position with a reason is accepted.
s: (d) One point for and one against

questions.q: Seema turns 18 and finds her name missing from the voters' list of her constituency. Which Act deals with the preparation and revision of electoral rolls and every citizen's right to vote from 18?
questions.a: The Representation of the People Act, 1950
o: The Representation of the People Act, 1950
The Representation of the People Act, 1951
The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952
The Anti-Defection Law of 1985

questions.q: A candidate offers a rival Rs 50,000 to withdraw from the contest. How does the chapter classify this?
questions.a: A corrupt practice listed under the Representation of the People Act, 1951
o: A corrupt practice listed under the Representation of the People Act, 1951
A permitted deal, since the rival agrees willingly
A delimitation matter under Article 82
A matter only for the Speaker of the House

questions.q: Constituency M has 5 lakh people and constituency N has 25 lakh, and each sends one MP. Which conclusion best fits the chapter?
questions.a: A person in M has five times the share of an MP that a person in N has, so equal representation is defeated
o: A person in M has five times the share of an MP that a person in N has, so equal representation is defeated
A person in N has five times the share of an MP that a person in M has
Both persons have an equal share, since each sends one MP
The difference does not matter because voters elect only parties

questions.q: During a campaign, which of these helpers is NOT among the government-related personnel whose assistance candidates are prohibited from taking?
questions.a: The candidate's cousin who runs a private shop
o: The candidate's cousin who runs a private shop
A police constable
A magistrate
An excise officer

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Constituency boundaries for the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha are redrawn from time to time through delimitation.
Reason (R): Once drawn, the boundaries of a constituency are fixed permanently by the Constitution.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about election laws and delimitation.
1. The Representation of the People Act, 1951 lists electoral offences and corrupt practices.
2. Constituency boundaries change over time depending on shifts in population density.
3. India has had four Delimitation Commissions.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
Match each item with what the chapter says about it.
1. RPA, 1950
2. RPA, 1951
3. Delimitation
4. Article 82
a. Rules for nomination, campaigns, voting and disputes
b. Mandates a Delimitation Commission
c. Allocation of seats and the preparation of electoral rolls
d. Fixing the territorial boundaries of constituencies
The Delimitation Commissions were set up in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002. The longest gap between two successive Commissions is ___ years.
True or False: A candidate who gives gifts to voters to make them vote, or not vote, commits a corrupt practice that the Representation of the People Act, 1951 lists. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The Act lists as an electoral offence any gift, offer or promise made by a candidate, or with the candidate's consent, to make a person contest, withdraw, vote or refrain from voting.
s: Reason: the 1951 Act lists any gift, offer or promise to influence contesting, withdrawing or voting

questions.q: A State has constituencies of 5 lakh and 25 lakh people. (a) How many times larger is the bigger one? (b) What does delimitation try to achieve in such a case?
questions.a: (a) 25 lakh / 5 lakh = 5 times. (b) It determines seats and fixes boundaries so that the ratio of seats to population is as close to equal as possible across constituencies.
s: (b) Seat to population ratio close to equal

questions.q: Differentiate between what the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Act of 1951 mainly deal with.
questions.a: The 1950 Act deals mainly with allocation of seats and delimitation, preparation and revision of electoral rolls, and the right of every citizen above 18 to vote. The 1951 Act deals with other aspects such as nomination, campaigns, voting procedures and disputes.
s: 1950: seats, rolls and right to vote

questions.q: (a) Work out the gaps in years between the successive Delimitation Commissions of 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002. (b) Which gap does the chapter ask students to find the reason for?
questions.a: (a) 11, 10 and 29 years. (b) The gap between 1973 and 2002.

questions.q: State any two corrupt practices listed in the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
questions.a: Any two of: a gift, offer or promise to make someone contest, withdraw, vote or not vote; an appeal to vote or not vote on grounds of religion, caste, race, community or language; taking assistance from government-related personnel.

questions.q: Farid says, 'Delimitation is needed because constituency boundaries are not permanently fixed, and Article 82 provides for a Delimitation Commission.' Is he right?
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the boundaries change over time with shifts in population density, and Article 82 mandates the establishment of a Delimitation Commission. Delimitation fixes the number of seats and the boundaries.

questions.q: Write a campaign incident for each of two corrupt practices from the chapter, naming the practice in each.
questions.a: Example: a candidate's agent promises Rs 2,000 to a voter to vote for him (gift or promise); a candidate asks voters of his own caste to vote for him (appeal on the basis of caste).
s: First incident describing a listed practice
Second incident describing a different practice

questions.q: Explain, with figures, how a gap between constituency sizes of 5 lakh and 25 lakh defeats the objective of equal representation.
questions.a: Both constituencies send one Member of Parliament. In the 5 lakh constituency each MP stands for fewer people, so each voter has five times the share of an MP compared with the 25 lakh constituency, since 25 / 5 = 5. Representation is therefore unequal.

questions.q: Explain how the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and 1951 together ensure the integrity, transparency and accountability of elections. Use one provision from each Act and one offence from the 1951 Act.
questions.a: The 1950 Act ensures that every citizen of 18 and above can vote without discrimination and that electoral rolls are prepared and revised, so the list of voters is open to check. The 1951 Act sets rules for nomination, campaigns and voting procedures, and resolves disputes, so process and results can be challenged. It also lists offences such as gifts or promises to voters. Together they make the process honest and answerable.
s: Linked to integrity, transparency or accountability

questions.q: A State has six constituencies with 15, 20, 25, 30, 40 and 50 lakh people. (a) Find the ideal population per constituency. (b) How many times is the largest constituency of the smallest? (c) Explain what delimitation would do.
questions.a: (a) Total 180 lakh / 6 = 30 lakh. (b) 50 / 15 = about 3.3 times. (c) It would redraw boundaries so that constituencies come close to 30 lakh each, bringing the ratio of seats to population close to equal.
s: (c) Delimitation explained as redrawing for equal ratio

questions.q:
A State has six Lok Sabha constituencies holding 15, 20, 25, 30, 40 and 50 lakh people. After a delimitation exercise the boundaries are redrawn and the six constituencies hold 28, 29, 30, 31, 31 and 31 lakh. A local leader from the 15 lakh constituency says her people will lose a familiar boundary and an MP who knows them.
(a) What is the State's total population, and what is the ideal population per constituency?
(b) By how many times did the gap between the largest and smallest constituency fall? Give both figures as ratios to one decimal place.
(c) The leader wants the old boundaries kept for another cycle. Take a side using the figures and the chapter's aim of delimitation.
questions.a: (a) 180 lakh; 30 lakh each. (b) Before: 50/15 = 3.3. After: 31/28 = 1.1. (c) Against keeping: the old gap defeats equal representation, where one MP stands for 50 lakh and another for 15 lakh. For keeping: familiarity of an MP with a known area, but the chapter's aim is equal ratio of seats to population. A reasoned choice with a cost is accepted.
s: (c) A side with figures and the chapter's aim

questions.q:
Forty-eight hours before polling in the Rohtas constituency, the Returning Officer receives three complaints. (i) A candidate promised Rs 5,000 to a rival to withdraw from the contest. (ii) At a rally a candidate asked voters 'of our caste' to vote for him. (iii) A police constable was seen helping to distribute a candidate's pamphlets. The office can send only one inspection team today.
(a) Which Act lists these matters, and what are they called?
(b) Which complaint is about assistance from government-related personnel?
(c) Which complaint should the team look at first? Defend your choice and say what waits.
questions.a: (a) The Representation of the People Act, 1951; they are corrupt practices or electoral offences. (b) Complaint (iii), police personnel. (c) Any choice with a reason: (i) first, since a withdrawal changes who stands and cannot be reversed once polling is near; or (ii) or (iii) first because a rally and uniformed help affect many voters. The others wait for the next day, which is the cost.
s: (c) A choice with a reason and what is delayed

questions.q: A State needs a Chief Electoral Officer to supervise election work. How, according to the chapter, is the officer appointed?
questions.a: By the ECI from among civil servants, in consultation with the State Government
o: By the ECI from among civil servants, in consultation with the State Government
By the State Government alone, from among the retired judges
By the Speaker of the Vidhan Sabha from among its members
By the District Magistrates who vote among themselves

questions.q: Hira sees a group handing out cash to voters near a polling area and wants to report it within minutes so a flying squad can reach the spot. Which ECI tool should she use?
questions.a: The cVIGIL App
o: The cVIGIL App
The Suvidha app
The Saksham App
ERONET

questions.q: Four residents: Anil (86 years old), Bhavna (a PwD with benchmark disability of 40 per cent), Chitra (80 years old) and Dev (a PwD with 25 per cent disability). Who qualifies for voting from home as extended in the 2024 General Elections?
questions.a: Anil and Bhavna
o: Anil and Bhavna
Anil, Bhavna and Chitra
Bhavna and Dev
All four of them

questions.q: An electoral roll lists Ramesh who has died, Sunita who is enrolled twice, and Imran who moved to another city; Pooja, who just turned 18, is missing. Which outcome fits the Special Intensive Revision?
questions.a: Delete Ramesh, Sunita's duplicate and Imran's old entry, and add Pooja
o: Delete Ramesh, Sunita's duplicate and Imran's old entry, and add Pooja
Add Ramesh, Sunita and Imran and delete Pooja
Delete only Ramesh, since the others are citizens
Delete nobody but add Pooja, since rolls are never corrected

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Independent candidates cannot contest elections in India.
Reason (R): Only political parties registered with the ECI can contest elections as parties.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Election Commission of India.
1. The ECI is an autonomous permanent constitutional body established on 25 January 1950.
2. Articles 324 to 329 of the Constitution provide for the establishment of the ECI and define its powers and duties.
3. At the State level, election work is supervised by the District Magistrate, who is appointed by the ECI.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: The ECI was established on 25 January 1950. On 25 January 2026 it completes ___ years.
Which of these is NOT a factor the chapter says the ECI must consider while deciding the election schedule?
questions.a: A ruling party's preferred date
o: A ruling party's preferred date
Weather conditions
The agricultural cycle
School and university examination schedules

questions.q: True or False: Voting from home for senior citizens above 85 years and persons with a benchmark disability of 40 per cent was extended across India for the first time in the 2024 General Elections. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says this was extended across India for the first time during the 2024 General Elections, as one of the ECI's initiatives to make elections more inclusive.
s: Reason: it was an inclusion initiative extended nationwide in 2024 for these two groups

questions.q: (a) Name two reasons for which the Special Intensive Revision deletes a voter's name. (b) Why does the ECI settle claims and objections before the final roll is published?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: death, change of residence, duplicate enrolment, being permanently untraceable. (b) So that no eligible citizen is left out and no ineligible person is included, giving people time to correct mistakes.
s: (b) Claims settled to avoid wrongful exclusion or inclusion

questions.q: (a) When does the ECI activate the machinery to conduct an election? (b) Name two factors it considers while deciding the schedule.
questions.a: (a) When the legislature's five-year term ends, or when it is dissolved before completing its term. (b) Any two of weather conditions, the agricultural cycle, school and university examination schedules, festivals.
s: (a) End of the term or early dissolution

questions.q: Differentiate between ETPBS and the cVIGIL App by saying who uses each and for what purpose.
questions.a: ETPBS lets service voters receive and cast postal ballots electronically from a place outside their constituency. cVIGIL lets voters report Model Code of Conduct violations and misconduct within minutes, so that flying squads act.
s: ETPBS: service voters, electronic postal ballot
cVIGIL: voters report violations for quick action

questions.q: Who can contest an election besides candidates of political parties, and what must a party do to be allotted a symbol according to the chapter?
questions.a: Independent candidates, who are not affiliated to any party, can contest. A party must be registered with the ECI and recognised as a national or state party to be allotted a symbol.
s: Registered and recognised national or state party gets a symbol

questions.q: Priya says, 'The ECI conducts only the Lok Sabha elections.' Is she right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The ECI conducts elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, Vidhan Sabha and Vidhan Parishad, and of the President and Vice President.
s: President and Vice President also named

questions.q: Write a situation in which the ECI acts as a quasi-judicial body, and say what it decides.
questions.a: Two groups of one party each claim the party's recognition and its election symbol. The ECI hears both and decides whom to recognise and who is to get the symbol.
s: A dispute about recognition or symbol
The ECI as the body that hears it

questions.q: Using the chapter, explain why holding an election is not enough for democracy by naming three situations that reduce its value.
questions.a: The chapter names candidates influenced by personal favours, votes counted inaccurately and some participants facing difficulty in voting because of accessibility. In each case elections happen but their democratic value falls, because the process must be inclusive, impartial and trustworthy.
s: Link to loss of public confidence or democratic value

questions.q: The questions at the end of the chapter ask which function of the ECI is most important for free and fair elections. List four functions and defend one as the most important.
questions.a: Functions: creating the electoral roll (with SIR), deciding the schedule and date, registering parties and allocating symbols, and ensuring free and fair elections. One may be defended: the roll, since only those on it may vote; or free and fair conduct, since without it elections lose public confidence. Credit goes to a reasoned choice.

questions.q: What is the Special Intensive Revision? Explain its objectives, the reasons for deletion and why it is necessary.
questions.a: It is an exercise by the ECI of updating, verifying and correcting the electoral rolls. Objectives: no eligible citizen left out and no ineligible person included, so young voters who just turned 18 are added. Names are deleted for death, change of residence, duplicate enrolment or being permanently untraceable. It is necessary because the rolls decide who may vote.
s: Definition: updating, verifying and correcting rolls
Objectives: no one eligible left out or ineligible included

questions.q:
A district has 15,00,000 names on its electoral roll. A Special Intensive Revision removes 12,000 voters who died, 21,000 who changed residence, 7,000 duplicate entries and 5,000 permanently untraceable voters. It also adds 38,000 young voters who turned 18. Polling is 60 days away, and one party asks the ECI to extend the period for claims and objections by two weeks.
(a) How many names are deleted in all?
(b) What is the number on the roll after the revision?
(c) Should the ECI grant the extension? Give a reason for each side and decide.
questions.a: (a) 12,000 + 21,000 + 7,000 + 5,000 = 45,000. (b) 15,00,000 - 45,000 + 38,000 = 14,93,000. (c) For the extension: more time to correct wrong deletions so no eligible citizen is left out. Against: the time before polling shrinks and the roll must be final in time. Either decision with a reason is accepted.
s: (c) Both sides stated and a decision

questions.q:
In a ward, 90 voters qualify for voting from home as senior citizens above 85 or as persons with a benchmark disability of 40 per cent. One official team can visit 15 homes a day, and 3 days are set aside. A second team would need one extra vehicle, costing Rs 8,000 (the Sugam app tracks such vehicles), and a team costs Rs 6,000 a day.
(a) Which two groups qualify, and how many homes can one team cover in 3 days?
(b) How many days would one team need for all 90?
(c) Compare the cost of two teams for 3 days with one team for 6 days.
(d) Which plan do you recommend and why?
questions.a: (a) Senior citizens above 85 and PwDs with a 40 per cent benchmark disability; 45 homes. (b) 90 / 15 = 6 days. (c) Two teams: 2 x 3 x 6,000 + 8,000 = Rs 44,000; one team: 6 x 6,000 = Rs 36,000. (d) Either: two teams cost Rs 8,000 more but finish in 3 days, leaving a margin before polling; one team is cheaper but runs 3 days longer, so the risk of missing someone before polling rises.
s: (d) A plan with the trade-off stated

questions.q: Mehul was elected to a Vidhan Sabha on a party's ticket. In an important vote he votes against the party's whip. What can the chapter's law lead to?
questions.a: He can be disqualified from the House, and the Speaker decides
o: He can be disqualified from the House, and the Speaker decides
He is automatically removed by the Election Commission
He keeps his seat, as the law covers only a change of party
He is barred from contesting any later election

questions.q: Four elected members acted as follows. Which one can the Anti-Defection Law reach?
questions.a: Sunita voluntarily gave up membership of the party on whose ticket she was elected
o: Sunita voluntarily gave up membership of the party on whose ticket she was elected
Tarun spoke in a debate with views that differed from the party's
Usha resigned as a committee member but stayed in the party
Vijay voted as the party's whip directed

questions.q: A student writes that the Janata Party formed the first coalition government at the national level in 1967. Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The alliances began in 1967, and the Janata Party's national coalition came in 1977
o: The alliances began in 1967, and the Janata Party's national coalition came in 1977
The alliances began in 1977, and the Janata Party government came in 1967
Both happened in 1985, with the Anti-Defection Law
Both happened in 1999, with the NDA and the UPA

questions.q: A legislator leaves her party because she believes its stand on a bill harms her district. Which description best fits the chapter's treatment of defection?
questions.a: It can be seen as opportunism against party discipline, or as upholding conscience
o: It can be seen as opportunism against party discipline, or as upholding conscience
It is always opportunism, since the chapter allows no other view
It is always an act of conscience, since the voter has no say
It is neither, because defection means only joining the ruling party

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A member who votes against the party's whip can be disqualified from the House.
Reason (R): The Anti-Defection Law aims to prevent defection and so provide stability to the elected government.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about parties, alliances and defection.
1. The era of alliances in India began only in 1977 with the Janata Party.
2. The Janata Party formed the first coalition government at the national level, against the backdrop of the National Emergency.
3. Under the Anti-Defection Law the Election Commission decides whether a member is disqualified.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Match each term with its description.
1. Defection
2. Independent candidate
3. Registered Unrecognised Political Party
4. Anti-Defection Law
a. A candidate not affiliated to any political party
b. A party that has never contested elections since registration, or lacks enough votes
c. Switching from the party under whose banner one was elected
d. Passed in 1985 through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment
The chapter says an era of alliances began in 1967 and the Janata Party formed a national coalition government in 1977. The gap between the two is ___ years.
True or False: Under the Anti-Defection Law, the Election Commission decides whether a member who gave up her party membership will be disqualified. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Speaker or Chairman of the House decides what needs to be done in such cases, not the Election Commission.
s: Correction: the Speaker or Chairman of the House decides

questions.q: (a) Name two ways in which political parties help voters during elections. (b) Why does the chapter call parties essential at the grassroots?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: enabling voters to make informed decisions, organising public opinion, campaigning on specific issues, offering meaningful choices. (b) They work directly at the grassroots level, where citizens meet candidates and learn about policies.
s: (b) Parties work directly at the grassroots

questions.q: Differentiate between the two views the chapter gives on defection.
questions.a: In the first view, defection is political opportunism when seen in the context of party discipline and political stability. In the other view, defection can be a way to uphold conscience or respond to changing public expectations.
s: Opportunism view tied to party discipline and stability

questions.q: (a) Which party led the first coalition at the Centre, and in which year? (b) Which two alliances have been the major ones since the late 1990s, and who led each?
questions.a: (a) The Janata Party, in 1977. (b) The NDA led by the BJP and the UPA led by the INC (until its dissolution in 2023).
s: (b) NDA with BJP and UPA with INC

questions.q: What does a multi-party system mean in India, and what does the chapter say it reflects?
questions.a: It means that many political parties exist and compete in elections. The chapter says it reflects the country's rich diversity of languages, cultures, religions and regions.

questions.q: Ria says, 'A member who votes against the party's whip is automatically disqualified.' How far is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says such a member can be disqualified, so the law covers this action. But it is not automatic: the Speaker or Chairman of the House decides what needs to be done in such cases.
s: The right part: voting against the whip can lead to disqualification
The wrong part: the Speaker or Chairman decides, it is not automatic

questions.q: Write two short situations: one in which a member could be disqualified under the law and one in which she could not. Give a reason for each.
questions.a: Could be: a member elected on party X's ticket voluntarily gives up its membership, which the law covers. Could not: a member votes as the party whip directs, since she neither gives up membership nor votes against the whip.

questions.q: Using the chapter's flow of party roles, explain what an opposition party does to ensure accountability.
questions.a: The chapter shows the winning party forming the government and implementing policies, while the opposition party participates in debates and committees. By questioning the government there, it ensures accountability.
s: Opposition takes part in debates and committees

questions.q: Trace the role of a political party over one election cycle, from organising public opinion to accountability, using the chapter's roles.
questions.a: A party organises public opinion and presents its agenda; it plans campaigns and prepares a manifesto and contests elections. Voters learn about issues and candidates through it. The winning party forms the government and formulates and implements policies, while the opposition ensures accountability through debates and committees. Citizens then judge the parties again at the next election.
s: Organising public opinion and presenting an agenda

questions.q: Argue for or against the statement: 'The Anti-Defection Law protects stability at the cost of conscience.' Use the chapter's two views of defection.
questions.a: The purpose of the law, passed in 1985 by the 52nd Amendment, is to prevent defection and so provide stability. It disqualifies a member who voluntarily gives up membership or votes against the whip. Supporting the statement: a member acting from conscience can lose the seat. Opposing it: the chapter calls defection political opportunism in the context of party discipline, so stability is worth protecting. Either side with both views mentioned earns marks.
s: The law's purpose and year stated

questions.q:
A Vidhan Sabha has 200 members. The ruling party has 108 and the opposition 92. On a bill, 9 ruling party members vote with the opposition because they believe it harms their district.
(a) How many votes make a majority in this House?
(b) How many votes does the bill get, how many go against it, and what is the result?
(c) The 9 are later disqualified for voting against the whip, so the House temporarily has 191 members. How many votes make a majority now, and does the ruling party still have one?
(d) Should the Speaker disqualify them? Weigh stability against conscience and decide.
questions.a: (a) 101. (b) For: 108 - 9 = 99; against: 92 + 9 = 101; the bill is defeated by 2. (c) Majority of 191 is 96; the ruling party has 99, so it still has a majority. (d) For disqualification: the law aims at stability and the members voted against the whip. Against: they may have acted on conscience for their district. Either decision with both considerations is accepted.
s: (c) 96 and the ruling party's 99 hold the majority

questions.q:
In a House of 300 seats, an alliance led by Party L (120 seats) includes Party M (20), Party N (12) and Party O (8). Party M has begun to disagree about a policy and threatens to leave.
(a) How many seats does the alliance hold, and how many are needed for a majority?
(b) If M alone leaves, does the alliance keep its majority? What if N alone leaves, or O alone?
(c) What should L do: give in to M's demand on the policy, or refuse? State the cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) 160 seats; 151 for a majority. (b) M leaves: 140, which is below 151, so the majority is lost. N leaves: 148, lost. O leaves: 152, kept. (c) Giving in keeps the government stable but L compromises on its own programme; refusing keeps its stand but risks losing the government. Either with a stated cost.

questions.q: Two days before polling, a forwarded message says the voting date has been changed and that voters should stay home. Which challenge from the chapter does this show, and how does the chapter say the ECI can respond?
questions.a: Fake news; through awareness campaigns, the Model Code of Conduct and the election laws
o: Fake news; through awareness campaigns, the Model Code of Conduct and the election laws
Intimidation; through delimitation of the constituency
Fake news; through a ban on all private messages
Misinformation; through voting by only senior citizens

questions.q: After pressing the button on the EVM, Lakshmi wants to be sure her vote went to the candidate she chose. Which measure named in the chapter lets her see this?
questions.a: The Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail slip
o: The Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail slip
The cVIGIL App
The electoral roll prepared polling-station-wise
The Voter Helpline App

questions.q: In one town, elections are held on schedule, but the polling hall has no ramp and a group of voters with disabilities cannot reach the booth. Which judgement fits the chapter?
questions.a: Elections happened, but their democratic value is reduced, since the process was not inclusive
o: Elections happened, but their democratic value is reduced, since the process was not inclusive
The election is fully democratic, since the date was announced in time
The election is invalid only if the ECI is not informed
The election gains value, since fewer people crowd the booth

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the measures the chapter names for addressing challenges to free and fair elections?
questions.a: A ban on political parties from campaigning
o: A ban on political parties from campaigning
The Model Code of Conduct
EVMs and VVPAT
Voter awareness campaigns

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The ECI uses EVMs and VVPAT as measures to address challenges to free and fair elections.
Reason (R): The Delimitation Commission was mandated by Article 82 of the Constitution.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the challenges to free and fair elections.
1. Casting a vote is a constitutional right, but the chapter does not describe it as a duty.
2. The ECI relies only on the Model Code of Conduct to meet challenges such as fake news and intimidation.
3. The Representation of the People Acts, the Delimitation Commission and the ECI together keep the election process free, fair and transparent.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: About 96.8 crore voters were eligible in 2024. If 60 per cent of them voted, the number who voted was ___ crore.
True or False: According to the chapter, an election held without addressing the accessibility needs of some voters still loses part of its democratic value. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that when some participants face difficulties in exercising their right to vote due to accessibility issues, elections may be held but their democratic value is reduced, because the process must be inclusive, impartial and trustworthy.
s: Reason: democracy needs an inclusive, impartial and trustworthy process, not only an election

questions.q: (a) Name the three challenges to free and fair elections shown on the chapter's road. (b) Name two measures with which the ECI addresses them.
questions.a: (a) Misinformation, fake news and intimidation. (b) Any two of: the RPA 1950 and 1951, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, VVPAT, voter awareness campaigns.

questions.q: In the chapter's story Ishani votes for the first time with her disabled brother. (a) Which two facilities helped him reach the polling booth? (b) What did she see after casting her vote, and what does it help voters check?
questions.a: (a) A wheelchair and volunteers who guided them. (b) The VVPAT slip, which lets a voter see that the vote was recorded as cast.
s: (b) VVPAT slip as a check on the vote

questions.q: Why does the chapter call elections 'the soul of democracy'? Give the reason it states.
questions.a: Because elections give every citizen an equal voice in the formation of a government, which is what democracy is meant to provide.
s: Every citizen gets an equal voice
Voice is used in forming a government

questions.q: The chapter says that 'constant vigilance and active citizen participation' can make elections more representative. Give one example of how a citizen can contribute, using an ECI tool.
questions.a: A citizen can report a Model Code of Conduct violation through the cVIGIL App within minutes so that a flying squad can act. This is citizen participation that keeps elections fair.
s: Linked to the tool and its effect on fairness

questions.q: Sana says, 'The ECI can ensure free and fair elections without any help from citizens.' Is she right?
questions.a: No. The chapter says that despite the ECI's measures, constant vigilance and active citizen participation are what make elections more representative and the democracy more robust. Citizens report violations through cVIGIL and vote.
s: The chapter's stress on vigilance and citizen participation

questions.q: Write a short example of misinformation that could appear before an election, then say how a voter could act on it using one tool named in the chapter.
questions.a: Example: a message claims that polling has been postponed in a ward. A voter can check with the Voter Helpline App for election information and updates, or report related misconduct on cVIGIL.
s: A tool named from the chapter

questions.q: From Ishani's polling day, identify three features that made voting inclusive and fair, and say which element of the chapter each fits.
questions.a: A wheelchair and volunteers (inclusion for persons with disabilities); identity checked with an alternative document when the voter ID and Aadhaar were forgotten (access with a valid proof); and the VVPAT slip (trust in the vote). Her grandmother voting from home shows inclusion of senior citizens.
s: Each tied to inclusion or trust

questions.q: What are the challenges to conducting free and fair elections in India? Explain how the ECI and the law respond to them and why citizens still matter.
questions.a: India has over 96.8 crore voters (in 2024), thousands of polling stations and hundreds of parties. Challenges include misinformation, fake news and intimidation. The ECI responds through the Representation of the People Acts 1950 and 1951, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, VVPAT and voter awareness campaigns. Citizens matter because constant vigilance and active participation make elections more representative.
s: Measures by the ECI and law

questions.q: 'Elections are the soul of democracy.' Do you agree? Support your view with three points from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes: elections give every citizen an equal voice in forming a government; casting a vote is a constitutional right and a duty; periodic elections make representatives accountable to the people. The laws, the Delimitation Commission and the ECI keep the process free, fair and transparent. A reasoned stance with three points earns full marks.
s: A reason linking the points to democracy

questions.q:
On polling day in Rampur constituency, the cVIGIL App receives 240 complaints. Of these, 30 per cent are about gifts or cash for voters, 25 per cent about intimidation, and the rest about posters and loudspeakers. Eight flying squads work two shifts, and each squad can attend 6 complaints in a shift.
(a) How many complaints are there in each of the three groups?
(b) How many complaints can the squads attend in all, and how many remain?
(c) Which group should the squads attend first? Defend your choice and say what the delay costs.
questions.a: (a) Gifts or cash: 72; intimidation: 60; posters and loudspeakers: 108. (b) 8 x 6 x 2 = 96 attended; 240 - 96 = 144 remain. (c) A choice with a reason: intimidation first, since it stops voters from voting at all; or gifts first, since they influence votes; the cost is that the 108 poster and loudspeaker complaints and others wait, so fewer cases are acted on in time.
s: (c) A choice defended, with the cost

questions.q:
In a ward with 1,500 voters, 60 per cent voted last time. The election officer has Rs 60,000. Plan 1: an awareness campaign aimed at raising the turnout to 75 per cent. Plan 2: ramps and Braille facilities that would enable 40 voters with disabilities to vote independently.
(a) How many voted last time, and how many more voters does a 75 per cent turnout need?
(b) If the target is met, what does each option cost per additional voter?
(c) Which option should the officer choose? Use the chapter's idea of inclusive elections and take a side.
questions.a: (a) 900 voted; 1,125 are needed at 75 per cent, so 225 more. (b) Plan 1: 60,000 / 225 = about Rs 267 per voter. Plan 2: 60,000 / 40 = Rs 1,500 per voter. (c) Either: Plan 1 reaches more voters per rupee; Plan 2 reaches people who cannot otherwise vote, and the chapter says an election that is not inclusive loses democratic value.
s: (c) A side taken using the chapter and the figures

questions.q: A polling officer turns Ishani away because she forgot both her voter ID card and her Aadhaar card. What does the chapter's account of her polling day show?
questions.a: Her identity was verified with an alternative document and she voted
o: Her identity was verified with an alternative document and she voted
She had to go home and return with the same two cards
She could vote only by applying for voting from home
She was allowed to vote with no identity check at all
